thread.title_full: 'You can create a world for yourself': Trey Roberts honored in the OUT100 - NewsBreak

author: Lauren Johnson
title: 'You can create a world for yourself': Trey Roberts honored in the OUT100 - NewsBreak
text:
By Lauren Johnson ,
5 hours ago
Long before Trey Roberts received national recognition for his advocacy and community work, he was a kid growing up in Hollister, North Carolina, imagining a bigger world for himself.
Roberts is an enrolled member of the Haliwa-Saponi Tribe and serves as outreach manager for the Triangle Native American Society.
He is also the lead organizer behind the Dix Park Inter-Tribal Pow Wow in Raleigh.
His work focuses on something deeply personal: creating spaces where people can see themselves, express themselves and feel connected to a community.
Roberts credits growing up in the Haliwa-Saponi community with helping shape the way he thinks about success and support.
"We're a small community that watches out and takes care of each other," he said, adding that his Native identity taught him to think about success in terms of the people around him and what a person gives back to the world.
That philosophy has carried into Roberts' work creating spaces for marginalized communities and advocating for greater visibility for Native people. He said Native people are too often talked about in the past tense, rather than as part of a thriving and evolving culture and community today.
Now Roberts' work is receiving national recognition. Roberts was selected as one of this year's OUT100 honorees . When he first learned the news, he wasn't entirely convinced it was real.
"I actually thought it was fake at first. I thought I was being scammed," Roberts recalled.
Then he put on his headphones, walked his usual trail, listened to Lady Gaga's "Edge of Glory" and cried. Roberts said the recognition brought with it a powerful feeling: being seen.
For him, however, the honor is also deeply connected to someone who isn't here to witness it. Roberts said the person who would be most proud is his grandmother, whom he called "Mama Deen."
Mama Deen - Trey Roberts' grandmother (Photo: Trey Roberts)
He said she instilled in him the belief that he could do something meaningful with his life and encouraged him until the end. He now carries her memory into his work.
And while Roberts is the one being honored, he hopes the recognition ultimately reaches someone else, particularly young LGBTQ+ people growing up in rural communities like the one where his own story began.
"I think to any queer kid growing up in a rural area, you get this idea like you can't see beyond the pines and you don't think you can go beyond it," Roberts said. "I want you to know, any queer kid who's living in the South, that you can create a world for yourself, and it can be something that people would love and celebrate."
Young Trey Roberts (Photo: Trey Roberts)
The OUT100 recognizes influential LGBTQ+ people and advocates.
ABC-owned television stations nominated eight people for the project this year, including Roberts as WTVD-TV Raleigh's honoree.

Roberts is an enrolled member of the Haliwa-Saponi Tribe and serves as outreach manager for the Triangle Native American Society. "We're a small community that watches out and takes care of each other," he said, adding that his Native identity taught him to think about success in terms of the people around him and what a person gives back to the world.
